newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian police seeks arrest of drug firm's staff.
newsitem.headline: Indian police seeks arrest of drug firm's staff.

text.p: Indian police ordered the arrest of 12 officials of a German multinational drugs firm over the alleged contamination of one of its drugs but a court temporarily halted the move, police said on Monday.
Police in the western Indian state of Maharashtra had issued arrest warrants against 12 employees of German multinational Boehringer Mannheim's Indian subsidiary.
The company however, over the weekend, obtained a court order restraining from arrest until October 10 when bail applications for 11 of the 12 accused will be heard, police said.
"Yes, we issued arrest warrants," Bipin Singh, deputy commissioner of police in Thane district, adjacent to Bombay, told Reuters on Monday.

He said this followed a complaint by the Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA) which accused the 12, including Boehringer Mannheim (India)'s expatriate managing director Paul Stinson, of "criminal negligence" in allowing contamination of an anti-bacterial medicine.
Police said Stinson is believed to have left the country for Canada.
At the Bombay office of the firm, it appeared to be business as usual. "There is no one here who can talk to the press," said the secretary to George Verghese, the marketing vice president.
"He's busy at a marketing meeting," she said of her boss.
Last week, FDA cancelled the licence of the company's Thane factory licence where Comsat Forte, the antibacterial tablet, was being produced.
"Samples tested by the FDA were found to contain anti-diabetic ingredient glibenclamide, which causes a drastic fall in blood pressure," the Times of India wrote on Sunday.

"FDA investigations showed that surplus stocks of glibenclamide amounting to 4.1 kg were lying unaccounted for in the unit's stores since November 1995." It quoted FDA officials as saying these stocks got mixed up with Comsat Forte ingredients during production.

"The drug was tested after 62 people turned critical after using it at an eye camp on August 16. Although the deadline for recall (of the drug from all markets given by FDA) expired on September 5, it claimed two lives in Kolar, Karnataka, five days later," the newspaper said.
Company officials and FDA commissioner Anil Lakhina were immediately unavailable for comment.
Boehringer Mannheim India had an annual turnover of over 500 million rupees ($14 million), drug industry officials said.
The company's shares fell on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Monday in reaction to the developments.
